goals: Explain what accounting ratios are, how they are expressed and why they are used
Classify ratios into liquidity, solvency, activity and profitability ratios
Compute and interpret the current ratio and the quick ratio, and the effect of transactions on them
Compute and interpret the debt-equity, total assets to debt, proprietary and interest coverage ratios

slides.narration: A figure in a balance sheet means little on its own. Are current liabilities of four lakh rupees large or small? It depends on what the company holds to pay them. Accounting ratios set two related figures side by side. In this part we learn what ratios are and why we use them, and then work out the liquidity and solvency ratios of an imagined company, Narmada Agro Foods.

slides.heading: What is an accounting ratio?
bullets: A ratio relates **two figures** from the financial statements.
**Ratio analysis**: computing, comparing and interpreting ratios.

visual.alt: Table of the three forms of expressing a ratio: a pure ratio such as two to one for liquidity and solvency, times such as ten times for turnover ratios, and a percentage such as twenty-five per cent for profitability ratios
visual.caption: Rounding rule in this chapter: two decimal places, rounded half up.

slides.narration: An accounting ratio is a relationship between two figures taken from the financial statements. It can be written in three ways: as a pure ratio, such as two to one for a current ratio; as a number of times, such as ten times for inventory turnover; or as a percentage, such as twenty-five per cent for a gross profit ratio. In this chapter every ratio is worked to two decimal places.

slides.heading: Why analyse ratios?

rows: it compares what can be turned into cash soon with what must be paid soon
it compares long-term debt with owners’ funds and assets
it shows how many times resources are turned into revenue
it relates profit to revenue and to capital employed
ratios of different years and firms can be set side by side
an unusual ratio points to the figure that needs attention

visual.alt: Table of objectives and advantages of ratio analysis: judge liquidity, judge solvency, measure efficiency, measure profitability, compare and plan, and locate weak spots

slides.narration: Why take the trouble? Ratios turn pages of figures into a few clear signals. They tell us whether a company can pay its short-term debts, whether its long-term structure is safe, how hard its resources are working and how much it earns. They let us compare years and firms, and they point management to weak spots. But they rest on past figures and cannot remove the effect of inflation.

Inventory, trade receivables, trade payables, fixed asset, net asset and working capital turnover
How much does the business earn?
Gross profit, operating, operating profit and net profit ratios; return on investment

slides.narration: Ratios fall into four families. Liquidity ratios ask whether short-term debts can be paid. Solvency ratios ask whether the long-term structure is safe. Activity ratios, also called turnover ratios, ask how efficiently resources are used. Profitability ratios ask how much the business earns. Each family speaks most to a different reader: creditors, lenders, management and shareholders.

slides.heading: Our case company: Narmada Agro Foods Ltd

visual.alt: Condensed balance sheet of Narmada Agro Foods as at 31 March 2026: shareholders' funds 15,00,000, non-current liabilities 6,00,000, current liabilities 4,00,000; non-current assets 17,00,000, current assets 8,00,000; total 25,00,000
visual.caption: An imagined company; sub-head totals only.

slides.narration: Meet Narmada Agro Foods, an imagined company in Jabalpur. Its balance sheet totals rupees twenty-five lakh. Shareholders' funds are rupees fifteen lakh, long-term debt is rupees six lakh and current liabilities are rupees four lakh. Non-current assets are rupees seventeen lakh and current assets rupees eight lakh. We will compute all its ratios from these figures and its statement of profit and loss.

slides.heading: Liquidity: the current ratio
bullets: Around **2 : 1** is the traditional comfort level.
Too low: dues may not be met. Too high: idle cash, slow stock or poor collection.

rows: Other current liabilities (outstanding expenses, unpaid dividend)
Current investments; short-term loans and advances
Prepaid expenses and other current assets

visual.alt: Table of what goes into the current ratio: inventories, trade receivables, cash, current investments, short-term advances and prepaid expenses over short-term borrowings, trade payables, other current liabilities and short-term provisions
visual.caption: Current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities; conventional level 2 : 1.

slides.narration: The current ratio divides current assets by current liabilities. Current assets are inventories, trade receivables, cash, current investments, short-term advances and prepaid expenses. Current liabilities are short-term borrowings, trade payables, other current liabilities and short-term provisions. Two to one is the traditional comfort level. Much lower may mean trouble paying bills; much higher may mean idle cash or unsold stock.

slides.heading: Liquidity: the quick (liquid) ratio

rows: Inventories: must be sold first, perhaps on credit
Prepaid expenses: will never come back as cash
Short-term loans and advances, other current assets

visual.alt: Table of quick assets: cash, trade receivables, current investments and short-term advances are kept; inventories and prepaid expenses are taken out
visual.caption: Quick ratio = quick assets ÷ current liabilities; conventional level 1 : 1.

slides.narration: The quick ratio is a sharper test. It keeps only the assets that can become cash almost at once. So we take current assets and remove inventories, which must first be sold, and prepaid expenses, which will never come back as cash. The result, quick assets, is divided by current liabilities. A quick ratio of one to one is the usual benchmark.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: liquidity ratios of Narmada
slides.body_md: Narmada (imagined): current assets ₹8,00,000, of which inventories ₹3,20,000 and prepaid expenses ₹40,000; current liabilities ₹4,00,000.

visual.alt: Working for the liquidity ratios of Narmada: current assets 8,00,000, quick assets 4,40,000, current liabilities 4,00,000; current ratio two to one, quick ratio one point one to one

slides.narration: For Narmada, current assets of rupees eight lakh divided by current liabilities of rupees four lakh give a current ratio of two to one. Quick assets are current assets less inventories and prepaid expenses, which leaves rupees four lakh forty thousand. Divided by current liabilities, that gives a quick ratio of one point one to one. Both meet the usual benchmarks, so Narmada can comfortably pay its short-term debts.

slides.heading: Quick check: the quick ratio
slides.narration: Complete the formula. Quick assets are compared with which group of liabilities?

slides.heading: How a transaction moves the current ratio
bullets: Recompute with the **new** figures; never guess.
With the ratio above 1, an equal rise in both parts lowers it and an equal fall raises it.

rows: Buys a machine for ₹80,000 in cash
Issues equity shares for ₹2,00,000 in cash

visual.alt: Table of the effect of five separate transactions on Narmada's current ratio of two to one: paying creditors raises it, buying goods on credit lowers it, collecting from customers leaves it unchanged, buying a machine for cash lowers it and issuing shares for cash raises it
visual.caption: Each transaction is taken separately, starting from 8,00,000 ÷ 4,00,000 = 2 : 1.

slides.narration: Transactions move ratios. Start from Narmada's current ratio of two to one. Paying a creditor lowers both parts by the same amount, and with the ratio above one, that raises it. Buying goods on credit raises both parts and lowers it. Collecting cash from a customer swaps one current asset for another, so nothing changes. Buying a machine for cash takes money out of current assets.

slides.heading: Quick check: paying the suppliers
slides.body_md: Work out the new current ratio after the payment.
slides.narration: Work out the new current assets and the new current liabilities after the payment, then divide.

slides.heading: Solvency: debt, equity and total assets

rows: more reliance on borrowed long-term funds: riskier for lenders
more assets behind each rupee of debt: safer for lenders
owners finance more of the assets: safer for outsiders
Profit before interest and tax ÷ Interest on long-term debt
interest is easier to pay out of profit

visual.alt: Table of the four solvency ratios with their formulas and what a higher figure means: debt-equity, total assets to debt, proprietary and interest coverage
visual.caption: Debt = long-term borrowings + long-term provisions; equity = shareholders' funds.

slides.narration: Solvency ratios look at the long term. Debt means long-term borrowings plus long-term provisions. Equity means shareholders' funds. The debt-equity ratio divides debt by equity; a lower figure means lenders are safer. The total assets to debt ratio shows how many rupees of assets stand behind each rupee of debt. The proprietary ratio shows what share of total assets the owners have financed.

slides.heading: Solvency: interest coverage

visual.alt: Working for interest coverage of Narmada: profit before interest and tax 4,00,000 divided by interest 50,000 gives eight times

slides.narration: The interest coverage ratio asks how many times the profit before interest and tax covers the interest on long-term debt. Narmada earns rupees four lakh before interest and tax and pays rupees fifty thousand of interest on its debentures, so interest is covered eight times. The higher the figure, the more easily the company can keep paying its lenders even if profits fall.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: solvency ratios of Narmada
slides.body_md: Narmada (imagined): share capital ₹10,00,000, reserves and surplus ₹5,00,000, 10% debentures ₹5,00,000, long-term provisions ₹1,00,000, total assets ₹25,00,000.

visual.alt: Working for the solvency ratios of Narmada: debt 6,00,000, equity 15,00,000, total assets 25,00,000; debt-equity zero point four to one, total assets to debt four point one seven to one, proprietary zero point six to one

slides.narration: Narmada's debt is rupees six lakh and its equity rupees fifteen lakh, so the debt-equity ratio is zero point four to one. Total assets of rupees twenty-five lakh divided by debt give four point one seven to one, after rounding. Equity divided by total assets gives a proprietary ratio of zero point six to one. Owners have financed most of the assets, so the long-term position is strong.

slides.heading: Quick check: what counts as debt?
slides.body_md: Choose the definition used in this chapter.
slides.narration: Think about which liabilities run for more than a year.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: finding missing figures
slides.body_md: An imagined company, **Dudhganga Dairy Ltd**, Kolhapur, has a current ratio of 2.6 : 1, a quick ratio of 1.4 : 1, inventories of ₹1,80,000 and no prepaid expenses. Find its current liabilities, current assets and quick assets.

rows: Gap between the ratios is caused by inventory

visual.alt: Steps for worked example 3: the gap of one point two between the current and quick ratios is caused by inventory of 1,80,000, so current liabilities are 1,50,000, current assets 3,90,000 and quick assets 2,10,000

slides.narration: Sometimes the ratios are given and a figure is missing. Dudhganga has a current ratio of two point six to one and a quick ratio of one point four to one, inventories of rupees one lakh eighty thousand and no prepaid expenses. The gap between the two ratios, one point two, comes only from inventory. So current liabilities are rupees one lakh fifty thousand, current assets rupees three lakh ninety thousand and quick assets rupees two lakh ten thousand. Recomputing both ratios confirms it.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Profit before interest and tax ÷ Interest on long-term debt

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: formulas of the current, quick, debt-equity, total assets to debt, proprietary and interest coverage ratios with the values for Narmada

slides.narration: To sum up: ratios relate two figures and are written as a proportion, in times or as a percentage. Liquidity ratios compare current or quick assets with current liabilities. Solvency ratios compare debt with equity and with total assets, equity with total assets, and profit before interest and tax with interest. Always see how a transaction changes both parts of a ratio before deciding whether it rises or falls.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Write **formula → working → answer**; each carries marks.
State the result in the right form: **x : 1**, **times** or **%**, to two decimal places.
Show **quick assets** and **debt** as separate workings.
For a transaction, **recompute** the ratio with the new figures and compare.
Missing figures: build equations from the ratios, then **recompute** the given ratios as a check.
slides.narration: In the exam, write the formula first, then the working, then the answer. State the result in the right form, to one, times or per cent, rounded to two decimal places. Show quick assets and debt as separate workings, because they carry marks. For a transaction question, recompute the ratio with the new figures rather than guessing, and check any missing figure by recomputing the given ratios.

goals: Compute inventory, trade receivables, trade payables, fixed asset, net asset and working capital turnover ratios
Work out capital employed in two ways and check that they agree
Compute the gross profit, operating, operating profit and net profit ratios and the return on investment

slides.heading: Activity and profitability ratios
slides.body_md: Part 2 — **turnover** ratios, **profitability** ratios, reading ratios together, and their **limitations**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: turnover ratios, cost of revenue and averages, capital employed both ways, profitability ratios, reading ratios together and limitations
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In part one we asked whether a company can pay its debts. Now we ask how well it uses its resources and how much it earns. Activity ratios measure how many times inventory, receivables, payables and assets are turned over in a year. Profitability ratios measure profit against revenue and against capital employed. We continue with Narmada Agro Foods, and end with how to read ratios and where they fall short.

slides.heading: Activity ratios: how hard do resources work?

visual.alt: Table of the six turnover ratios, each a flow of the year over a resource: inventory, trade receivables, trade payables, fixed asset, net asset and working capital turnover
visual.caption: All are expressed in times. Average = (opening + closing) ÷ 2.

slides.narration: Every activity ratio sets a flow of the year against the resource behind it. Inventory turnover sets the cost of revenue from operations against average inventory. Receivables turnover sets credit revenue against average trade receivables. Payables turnover sets credit purchases against average trade payables. Fixed asset, net asset and working capital turnover set revenue from operations against those resources. Each is expressed in times.

slides.heading: Cost of revenue from operations and average inventory

visual.alt: Working of the cost of revenue from operations of Narmada: opening inventory plus purchases plus direct expenses less closing inventory equals 30,00,000, which is also revenue less gross profit; average inventory 3,00,000

slides.narration: Inventory is valued at cost, so inventory turnover uses the cost of revenue from operations, not revenue. For Narmada, opening inventory plus purchases plus direct expenses, less closing inventory, gives a cost of rupees thirty lakh. That also equals revenue less gross profit. Average inventory is the opening and closing figures added together and halved, which gives rupees three lakh.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: inventory, receivables and payables turnover
slides.body_md: Narmada (imagined): credit revenue ₹32,00,000; credit purchases ₹24,00,000; trade receivables ₹2,60,000 at the start and ₹2,80,000 at the end of the year; trade payables ₹2,60,000 and ₹2,40,000.

visual.alt: Working for the inventory, trade receivables and trade payables turnover of Narmada: ten times, eleven point eight five times and nine point six times
visual.caption: Credit revenue ₹32,00,000; credit purchases ₹24,00,000.

slides.narration: Narmada's inventory turned over ten times in the year. Credit revenue of rupees thirty-two lakh against average trade receivables of rupees two lakh seventy thousand gives eleven point eight five times, after rounding. Credit purchases of rupees twenty-four lakh against average trade payables of rupees two lakh fifty thousand give nine point six times. Customers pay Narmada a little faster than Narmada pays its suppliers, which is a comfortable position.

slides.heading: Quick check: the cost of revenue
slides.body_md: Choose how the cost of revenue from operations is found.
slides.narration: Gross profit is what is left of revenue after one particular cost. Which one?

slides.heading: Capital employed: two routes, one answer

rows: Add: Working capital (current assets − current liabilities)

visual.alt: Capital employed of Narmada worked out two ways: shareholders' funds plus non-current liabilities, and non-current assets plus working capital, both give 21,00,000
visual.caption: The two routes must agree; if they do not, an item has been misplaced.

slides.narration: Capital employed is the long-term money in the business. From the liabilities side it is shareholders' funds plus non-current liabilities: for Narmada, rupees twenty-one lakh. From the assets side it is non-current assets plus working capital, and that gives exactly the same figure. If your two answers differ, an item has been put in the wrong place.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: fixed asset, net asset and working capital turnover
slides.body_md: Narmada (imagined): revenue from operations ₹40,00,000; net fixed assets ₹16,00,000; capital employed ₹21,00,000; working capital ₹4,00,000.

visual.alt: Working for the fixed asset, net asset and working capital turnover of Narmada: two point five times, one point nine times and ten times

slides.narration: Revenue from operations of rupees forty lakh is two point five times the net fixed assets of rupees sixteen lakh, one point nine times the capital employed after rounding, and ten times the working capital of rupees four lakh. A higher turnover means the same resources are producing more revenue, so these ratios are best compared with earlier years and with similar firms.

slides.heading: Quick check: match the formulas
slides.body_md: Match each turnover ratio with its formula.
slides.narration: For each ratio, ask which flow of the year and which resource are being compared.

slides.heading: Profitability: the operating statement

rows: Less: Cost of revenue from operations
Less: Loss on sale of machinery

visual.alt: Operating statement of Narmada: revenue 40,00,000, gross profit 10,00,000, operating profit 4,00,000, profit before interest and tax 4,00,000, profit before tax 3,50,000 and profit after tax 2,45,000
visual.caption: Interest received and the loss on sale of machinery are non-operating.

slides.narration: Profitability ratios are measured on revenue from operations. Narmada's gross profit is rupees ten lakh. Taking away operating expenses, that is employee benefits, depreciation and other operating costs, leaves an operating profit of rupees four lakh. Non-operating items, such as interest received and a loss on selling a machine, come next, giving profit before interest and tax. Then interest and tax leave the profit after tax.

visual.caption: Segment widths are computed from the operating statement.

slides.narration: Think of every hundred rupees of revenue. For Narmada, seventy-five rupees go on the cost of revenue from operations and fifteen rupees on operating expenses. That makes an operating ratio of ninety per cent. What is left, ten rupees, is operating profit, so the operating profit ratio is ten per cent. The two always add up to one hundred.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: profitability ratios of Narmada
slides.body_md: Narmada (imagined): revenue from operations ₹40,00,000; gross profit ₹10,00,000; operating profit ₹4,00,000; profit before interest and tax ₹4,00,000; profit before tax ₹3,50,000; profit after tax ₹2,45,000; capital employed ₹21,00,000.

visual.alt: Working for the profitability ratios of Narmada: gross profit twenty-five per cent, operating ratio ninety per cent, operating profit ratio ten per cent, net profit after tax six point one three per cent, before tax eight point seven five per cent, return on investment nineteen point zero five per cent

slides.narration: Narmada's gross profit ratio is twenty-five per cent. Its net profit ratio after tax is six point one three per cent after rounding, and before tax it is eight point seven five per cent. Return on investment divides profit before interest and tax by capital employed: rupees four lakh on rupees twenty-one lakh, which is nineteen point zero five per cent. That is well above the ten per cent interest it pays on its debentures.

slides.heading: Quick check: operating profit ratio
slides.body_md: Use the link between the two operating ratios.
slides.narration: Operating cost and operating profit together make up the whole of revenue from operations.

slides.heading: Reading the ratios together

rows: Can pay current dues without selling stock
Stock sold about every five weeks
Long-term funds earn more than they cost

visual.alt: Interpretation table for Narmada: current and quick ratios meet the conventions, borrowing is modest and interest well covered, inventory turns over ten times a year, and return on investment is above the cost of borrowing
visual.caption: A ratio is read against a benchmark, a past year or similar firms.

slides.narration: A ratio means something only when it is compared: with a benchmark, with last year, or with similar firms. Narmada's liquidity meets the usual benchmarks, its debt is modest and well covered, its stock turns over ten times a year, and it earns a healthy return on capital employed. A single figure is never the whole story, so read the four families together.

slides.heading: Limitations of ratio analysis

rows: Ratios describe what has happened, not what will happen
Old assets at cost make turnover and returns look higher
Skill of managers, morale and brand do not show in ratios
Depreciation or inventory methods differ between firms
Year-end figures can be tidied up to flatter the ratios
A healthy figure for one industry may be weak for another

visual.alt: Table of limitations of ratio analysis: past figures, inflation ignored, qualitative factors left out, different accounting policies, window dressing and no universal standard

slides.narration: Ratios have limits. They come from past figures and ignore inflation. They leave out quality, such as the skill of managers. Firms use different accounting policies, so their ratios are not always comparable. Year-end figures can be dressed up. And there is no single correct value for most ratios: what is healthy for a retailer may be poor for a steel plant.

slides.heading: Quick check: a tidy year end
slides.narration: Think about what happens if a company tidies up its figures just before the balance sheet date.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 2

rows: Cost of revenue from operations ÷ Average inventory
Credit revenue from operations ÷ Average trade receivables
Net credit purchases ÷ Average trade payables
Revenue from operations ÷ Net fixed assets

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 2: formulas of the six turnover ratios and the five profitability ratios with the values for Narmada

slides.narration: To sum up: activity ratios divide a flow of the year by the resource behind it and are expressed in times, using averages for inventory, receivables and payables. Capital employed is shareholders' funds plus non-current liabilities, and must equal non-current assets plus working capital. Profitability ratios are percentages of revenue from operations, except return on investment, which relates profit before interest and tax to capital employed.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Inventory turnover uses **cost** of revenue from operations and **average** inventory.
Use **credit** revenue and **credit** purchases for receivables and payables turnover (total, if credit is not given).
Leave **non-operating** items out of the operating ratio.
Add back **interest and tax** to reach profit before interest and tax.
Compute **capital employed both ways** as a check.
slides.narration: Use the cost of revenue from operations for inventory turnover, credit figures for receivables and payables, and averages wherever opening and closing figures are given. Leave non-operating items out of the operating ratio. Add back interest and tax to reach profit before interest and tax. Compute capital employed both ways as a check. And when you interpret, compare with a benchmark or with last year.

sections.heading: 2. One set of definitions and the rounding rule
sections.body_md:
**Definitions.** The table sets out what each base means in this chapter, and the second table gives all seventeen formulas. Note especially:
- **Debt** is the non-current liabilities only; current liabilities never enter solvency ratios.
- **Capital employed** can be worked out from either side of the balance sheet; the two answers must be equal, which is a useful check.
- **Operating expenses** do not include finance costs or non-operating losses (loss on sale of a fixed asset, loss by fire); non-operating income (interest or dividend received, profit on sale of an asset) is also left out of operating profit.
- When credit revenue or credit purchases are not given, the total figure is used; when only closing figures are given, they replace the average.

**Rounding rule.** Ratios are worked to **two decimal places**, rounded half up (1.2667 → 1.27; 6.125 → 6.13). An exact result is written as it is (2.5 : 1, 25%). Write liquidity and solvency ratios as "x : 1", turnover ratios and interest coverage in "times", and profitability ratios as percentages.

sections.heading: 4. Solvency ratios
sections.body_md:
**Debt-equity ratio = debt ÷ equity** (debt = long-term borrowings + long-term provisions; equity = shareholders' funds). A low ratio means a larger safety margin for lenders; a high ratio means heavy dependence on borrowed funds and a larger fixed interest burden.

**Total assets to debt ratio = total assets ÷ debt.** The higher it is, the better covered the long-term lenders are.

**Proprietary ratio = shareholders' funds ÷ total assets.** It shows the share of assets financed by owners; a higher ratio means greater long-term safety for creditors.

**Interest coverage ratio = profit before interest and tax ÷ interest on long-term debt** (in times). It shows how many times interest is earned; a high figure reassures lenders that interest will be paid even if profits fall.

sections.heading: 5. Activity (turnover) ratios
sections.body_md:
- **Inventory turnover = cost of revenue from operations ÷ average inventory.** A higher figure means faster-moving stock; a very high one can mean stock too thin to meet demand.
- **Trade receivables turnover = credit revenue from operations ÷ average trade receivables.** Higher means quicker collection.
- **Trade payables turnover = net credit purchases ÷ average trade payables.** Higher means suppliers are paid quickly; lower means the firm takes longer credit.
- **Fixed asset turnover = revenue from operations ÷ net fixed assets.**
- **Net asset (capital employed) turnover = revenue from operations ÷ capital employed.**
- **Working capital turnover = revenue from operations ÷ working capital.**

All are in **times**. Revenue from operations is net of sales returns; credit purchases are net of purchases returns.

sections.body_md:
- **Gross profit ratio = gross profit ÷ revenue from operations × 100.**
- **Operating ratio = (cost of revenue from operations + operating expenses) ÷ revenue from operations × 100.**
- **Operating profit ratio = operating profit ÷ revenue from operations × 100 = 100 − operating ratio.**
- **Net profit ratio = net profit ÷ revenue from operations × 100**, computed on profit before tax or on profit after tax as the question asks.
- **Return on investment (return on capital employed) = profit before interest and tax ÷ capital employed × 100.**

Gross and operating ratios ignore non-operating items; the net profit ratio includes them. Return on investment uses profit before interest because capital employed includes the lenders’ money.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Using **revenue** instead of **cost of revenue from operations** in inventory turnover, or closing instead of **average** inventory.
- Leaving **bills receivable / bills payable** out of trade receivables and trade payables, or using total instead of **credit** figures when credit figures are given.
- Taking **current liabilities** into debt in the debt-equity ratio.
- Forgetting to remove **prepaid expenses** (as well as inventories) from quick assets.
- Including **non-operating** items (loss on sale of an asset, interest received) in the operating ratio.
- Using profit after tax in **return on investment** or **interest coverage**: both need profit before interest and tax.
- Writing the answer in the wrong form (25 instead of 25%, 2 instead of 2 : 1) or not rounding to two decimal places.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: one formula, one effect of a transaction, or one ratio in an MCQ.
- 3 marks: two or three ratios, about 1 mark each (formula and working ½, answer ½), or a missing-figure chain.
- 4 marks: four ratios, or the effect of four transactions (1 mark each with the reason).
- 6 marks: five or six ratios from a balance sheet and statement of profit and loss, or a missing-figure problem; bases such as capital employed carry their own marks.

questions.stem_md: A newspaper column claims that "ratios tell an investor all there is to know about a company". Explain any three limitations of ratio analysis that the columnist has overlooked.
questions.solution_md: Any three limitations, each explained in a sentence or two.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Based on historical figures:** ratios are computed from past financial statements, so they say little directly about the future.
2. **Ignore price-level changes:** assets bought years ago stay at cost, so ratios such as fixed asset turnover or return on investment can look better (or worse) than the real position.
3. **Ignore qualitative factors:** the quality of management, labour relations or the loyalty of customers cannot be expressed as ratios, though they decide the future of a business.
4. *(Also accepted)* Different accounting policies make comparison between firms unreliable; window dressing on the balance sheet date can distort ratios; there is no single correct standard for most ratios; a ratio is only as reliable as the statements behind it.

questions.stem_md: The directors of an imagined company, Uttarvahini Spinners Ltd, are new to financial analysis. Explain to them (a) what accounting ratios and ratio analysis are, and (b) any four objectives of ratio analysis.
questions.solution_md: Define both terms, mention the three forms of expression, then give four objectives, each with a line of explanation.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a) Meaning.** An **accounting ratio** is a mathematical relationship between two related figures taken from the financial statements, such as current assets and current liabilities. It can be expressed as a pure ratio (2 : 1), as a number of times (8 times) or as a percentage (25%). **Ratio analysis** is the process of computing such ratios, comparing them over years, with other firms or with standards, and interpreting them to judge the liquidity, solvency, efficiency and profitability of a business.

**(b) Objectives:**
1. **To judge liquidity:** whether the company can meet its short-term obligations out of its current assets.
2. **To judge solvency:** whether its long-term financial structure is sound and whether it can pay interest and repay long-term debt.
3. **To measure operating efficiency:** how quickly inventory, receivables and assets are turned into revenue.
4. **To measure profitability:** what the company earns on its revenue and on the capital employed in it.
5. *(Also accepted)* To simplify accounting figures; to make inter-firm and inter-period comparison possible; to help in planning and forecasting; to locate weak spots for corrective action.

| Prepaid expenses | 15,000 |
| Current investments | 25,000 |
| Trade payables | 1,80,000 |
| Bills payable | 30,000 |
| Outstanding wages | 20,000 |
| Provision for tax (short-term) | 50,000 |
| 9% Debentures | 4,00,000 |
| Provision for gratuity (long-term) | 60,000 |
questions.solution_md: Separate the current items from the non-current ones first; take inventories and prepaid expenses out of current assets for the quick ratio.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Working | ₹ |
| --- | ---: |
| Current assets: inventories + trade receivables + bills receivable + cash at bank + prepaid expenses + current investments | 5,50,000 |
| Current liabilities: trade payables + bills payable + outstanding wages + provision for tax | 2,80,000 |
| Quick assets: current assets − inventories − prepaid expenses | 2,95,000 |

- Current ratio = Current assets ÷ Current liabilities = 5,50,000 ÷ 2,80,000 ≈ 1.96 : 1
- Quick ratio = Quick assets ÷ Current liabilities = 2,95,000 ÷ 2,80,000 ≈ 1.05 : 1

The debentures and the provision for gratuity are non-current liabilities and are left out of both ratios.

questions.stem_md: Koyna Castings Ltd, an imagined foundry, has a current ratio of 2.8 : 1, a quick ratio of 1.5 : 1 and working capital of ₹3,60,000. It has no prepaid expenses. Calculate its current liabilities, current assets and inventories.
questions.solution_md: Express working capital in terms of current liabilities first; with no prepaid expenses, inventories are the only gap between current and quick assets.

answer.model_answer_md:
- Working capital = current assets − current liabilities = 2.8L − L = 1.8L, where L is current liabilities. So L = 3,60,000 ÷ 1.8 = **₹2,00,000**.
- Current assets = 2.8 × 2,00,000 = **₹5,60,000**.
- Quick assets = 1.5 × 2,00,000 = 3,00,000.
- Inventories = current assets − quick assets = 5,60,000 − 3,00,000 = **₹2,60,000**.

Check: 5,60,000 ÷ 2,00,000 = 2.8 : 1; 3,00,000 ÷ 2,00,000 = 1.5 : 1.

questions.stem_md:
Kabini Coffee Curing Ltd, an imagined company, has current assets of ₹4,00,000 and current liabilities of ₹2,00,000. Taking each transaction separately, state with reasons whether its current ratio will increase, decrease or not change, and show the new ratio:

(i) Paid trade payables ₹50,000.
(ii) Bought goods on credit for ₹40,000.
(iii) Collected ₹25,000 from trade receivables.
(iv) Bought a coffee roaster (machinery) for ₹30,000 in cash.
questions.solution_md: Trace each transaction to current assets and current liabilities, recompute, then compare with the original ratio.

answer.model_answer_md:
Current ratio before the transactions = 4,00,000 ÷ 2,00,000 = 2 : 1.

| Transaction | Change in current assets | Change in current liabilities | New ratio | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| (i) Paid trade payables ₹50,000 | −50,000 | −50,000 | 3,50,000 ÷ 1,50,000 ≈ 2.33 : 1 | **Increases** |
| (ii) Bought goods on credit for ₹40,000 | +40,000 | +40,000 | 4,40,000 ÷ 2,40,000 ≈ 1.83 : 1 | **Decreases** |
| (iii) Collected ₹25,000 from trade receivables | No change | No change | 4,00,000 ÷ 2,00,000 = 2 : 1 | **No change** |
| (iv) Bought a coffee roaster (machinery) for ₹30,000 in cash | −30,000 | No change | 3,70,000 ÷ 2,00,000 = 1.85 : 1 | **Decreases** |

Reasons: (i) both sides fall by the same amount, and with the ratio above 1 that raises it; (ii) both sides rise by the same amount, which lowers a ratio above 1; (iii) one current asset (cash) replaces another (receivables); (iv) cash, a current asset, is turned into a non-current asset.

questions.stem_md: While working out the debt-equity ratio of an imagined company, Subarnarekha Metals Ltd, its accountant has to decide what "debt" means. Under the definitions used in this chapter, debt is

options.text_md: all liabilities, current and non-current
trade payables and short-term borrowings only
share capital plus reserves and surplus
long-term borrowings plus long-term provisions

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** long-term borrowings plus long-term provisions. Debt means the long-term funds owed to outsiders, the non-current liabilities; equity means shareholders' funds. Current liabilities are left out of this ratio.

questions.stem_md: Mahi Plastics Ltd, an imagined company, has long-term debt of ₹4,00,000 and shareholders' funds of ₹8,00,000. It issues fresh equity shares of ₹2,00,000 for cash. Its debt-equity ratio will

options.text_md: fall to 0.25 : 1
fall to 0.4 : 1
rise to 0.75 : 1
stay at 0.5 : 1

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** fall to 0.4 : 1. Equity rises to 10,00,000 while debt is unchanged: 4,00,000 ÷ 10,00,000 = 0.4 : 1, lower than 0.5 : 1.

questions.stem_md: Luni Salt Works Ltd, an imagined company, has 12% debentures of ₹10,00,000. Its profit after charging debenture interest but before tax is ₹4,80,000. Its interest coverage ratio is

options.text_md: 5 times
4 times
0.2 times
12 times

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 5 times. Interest = 12% of 10,00,000 = 1,20,000. Profit before interest and tax = 4,80,000 + 1,20,000 = 6,00,000. Coverage = 6,00,000 ÷ 1,20,000 = 5 times.

questions.stem_md: The proprietary ratio of an imagined company, Ravi Hosiery Ltd, has risen from 0.45 : 1 to 0.7 : 1 over three years. For its creditors and lenders this means that

options.text_md: the company now depends more on borrowed funds than before
a larger share of its total assets is now financed by the owners, so outsiders are better protected
the company’s profit has risen in the same proportion
its current assets have grown faster than its current liabilities

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** a larger share of its total assets is now financed by the owners, so outsiders are better protected. The proprietary ratio is shareholders' funds ÷ total assets; a higher figure means owners' money backs more of the assets, leaving a wider cushion for outsiders.

questions.stem_md: Jhelum Willow Bats Ltd, an imagined company in Anantnag, has: equity share capital ₹8,00,000; general reserve ₹2,00,000; surplus in the Statement of Profit and Loss ₹1,00,000; 10% debentures ₹3,00,000; long-term provision for warranties ₹1,40,000; trade payables ₹2,00,000. Compute its debt-equity ratio.

Beas Woollens Ltd, an imagined company in Kullu, shows: share capital ₹5,00,000; reserves and surplus ₹2,00,000; long-term borrowings ₹5,00,000; long-term provisions ₹1,00,000; current liabilities ₹2,00,000; property, plant and equipment ₹9,00,000; non-current investments ₹1,50,000; current assets ₹4,50,000. Compute its total assets to debt ratio.
True or false? Other things being equal, a bank lending to an imagined company, Krishna Pulses Ltd, is safer when the company’s debt-equity ratio is 0.3 : 1 than when it is 1.5 : 1.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** A lower ratio means owners have put in more of the long-term funds, so there is a larger margin of safety for lenders and a smaller fixed burden of interest.

questions.stem_md: Unlike the current ratio, which is written as a proportion such as 2 : 1, the interest coverage ratio of a company is normally expressed in ___.
questions.solution_md: It is stated in times: profit before interest and tax is so many times the interest on long-term debt.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The interest coverage ratio is worked out on profit before interest and tax, not on profit after tax.

**Reason (R):** Interest on long-term debt is a charge met before tax is worked out, so the whole profit before interest and tax is available to pay it.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true and R explains A: since interest is paid before tax, the profit that "covers" it is the profit before both interest and tax.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A total assets to debt ratio of 5 : 1 means that every rupee of long-term debt is backed by five rupees of assets.

**Reason (R):** The higher the total assets to debt ratio, the less secure the long-term lenders are.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true. R is false: more assets behind each rupee of debt means lenders are better protected, not less.

questions.stem_md: The balance sheet of Vamsadhara Cashew Exports Ltd, an imagined company in Srikakulam, shows on 31 March 2026: equity share capital ₹10,00,000; reserves and surplus ₹2,00,000; long-term borrowings ₹6,00,000; trade payables ₹3,00,000; short-term provisions ₹1,00,000; property, plant and equipment ₹14,00,000; inventories ₹3,50,000; trade receivables ₹3,00,000; cash and cash equivalents ₹1,50,000. Compute the debt-equity ratio, the total assets to debt ratio and the proprietary ratio.
questions.solution_md: Find debt, equity and total assets first; then each ratio is one division. Round to two decimal places.

answer.model_answer_md:
Debt = 6,00,000; equity (shareholders' funds) = 10,00,000 + 2,00,000 = 12,00,000; total assets = 14,00,000 + 3,50,000 + 3,00,000 + 1,50,000 = 22,00,000 (equal to the total of equity and liabilities).

| Ratio | Formula | Working | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Debt-equity | Debt ÷ Equity (shareholders' funds) | 6,00,000 ÷ 12,00,000 = 0.5 : 1 | **0.5 : 1** |
| Total assets to debt | Total assets ÷ Debt | 22,00,000 ÷ 6,00,000 ≈ 3.67 : 1 | **3.67 : 1** |
| Proprietary | Shareholders' funds ÷ Total assets | 12,00,000 ÷ 22,00,000 ≈ 0.55 : 1 | **0.55 : 1** |

questions.stem_md: Chaliyar Plywood Ltd, an imagined company in Nilambur, earned a profit after tax of ₹3,15,000 for the year. Tax is charged at 30% of profit before tax. It has ₹5,00,000 of 10% debentures outstanding for the whole year. Compute its interest coverage ratio.
questions.solution_md: Work back from profit after tax: add back tax, then interest; divide by the interest.

answer.model_answer_md:
- Profit before tax = 3,15,000 × 100 ÷ 70 = 4,50,000 (tax 1,35,000).
- Interest on debentures = 10% of 5,00,000 = 50,000.
- Profit before interest and tax = 4,50,000 + 50,000 = 5,00,000.
- Interest coverage ratio = Profit before interest and tax ÷ Interest on long-term debt = 5,00,000 ÷ 50,000 = 10 times.

questions.stem_md:
Mandovi Fisheries Ltd, an imagined company in Goa, has long-term debt of ₹6,00,000 and shareholders' funds of ₹12,00,000. Taking each transaction separately, state whether its debt-equity ratio will increase, decrease or not change, and show the new ratio:

(i) Issued equity shares for ₹2,00,000 in cash.
(ii) Raised a long-term loan of ₹3,00,000.
(iii) Bought a fishing trawler for ₹1,00,000 in cash.
(iv) Paid a cash dividend of ₹60,000 out of the surplus in its Statement of Profit and Loss.
questions.solution_md: Ask of each transaction: does it change long-term debt, shareholders’ funds, both or neither? Then recompute.

answer.model_answer_md:
Debt-equity ratio before the transactions = 6,00,000 ÷ 12,00,000 = 0.5 : 1.

| Transaction | Change in debt | Change in equity | New ratio | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| (i) Issued equity shares for ₹2,00,000 in cash | No change | +2,00,000 | 6,00,000 ÷ 14,00,000 ≈ 0.43 : 1 | **Decreases** |
| (ii) Raised a long-term loan of ₹3,00,000 | +3,00,000 | No change | 9,00,000 ÷ 12,00,000 = 0.75 : 1 | **Increases** |
| (iii) Bought a fishing trawler for ₹1,00,000 in cash | No change | No change | 6,00,000 ÷ 12,00,000 = 0.5 : 1 | **No change** |
| (iv) Paid a cash dividend of ₹60,000 out of the surplus in its Statement of Profit and Loss | No change | −60,000 | 6,00,000 ÷ 11,40,000 ≈ 0.53 : 1 | **Increases** |

Reasons: (i) only equity rises; (ii) only debt rises; (iii) one asset replaces another, neither debt nor equity moves; (iv) the dividend reduces the surplus, and so the equity, while debt stays the same.

questions.stem_md:
Alaknanda Herbals Ltd, an imagined company in Rishikesh, gives the following on 31 March 2026. The debentures were outstanding for the whole year. Compute (a) the debt-equity ratio, (b) the total assets to debt ratio, (c) the proprietary ratio and (d) the interest coverage ratio, and (e) comment briefly on its long-term solvency.

| Reserves and surplus | 5,00,000 |

| Trade receivables | 3,50,000 |
| Cash and cash equivalents | 2,00,000 |
| Prepaid expenses | 50,000 |
| Profit before tax for the year | 6,24,000 |
questions.solution_md: Fix the three bases first (equity, debt, total assets); interest comes from the debenture rate; profit before interest and tax is profit before tax plus that interest.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Workings**

| Item | ₹ |
| --- | ---: |
| Equity (shareholders' funds) = share capital + reserves and surplus | 20,00,000 |
| Debt = 12% debentures + long-term provisions | 10,00,000 |

questions.stem_md: An imagined trader, Palar Footwear Ltd, knows its revenue from operations and its gross profit for the year, but not its purchases. To compute its inventory turnover ratio it needs the cost of revenue from operations, which equals

options.text_md: revenue from operations plus gross profit
closing inventory less opening inventory
revenue from operations less gross profit
gross profit divided by revenue from operations

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** revenue from operations less gross profit. Gross profit is what remains of revenue after the cost of the goods sold, so that cost is revenue minus gross profit.

questions.stem_md: Penganga Spices Ltd, an imagined company, had revenue from operations of ₹12,00,000 and a cost of revenue from operations of ₹9,60,000. Its inventory was ₹1,10,000 at the start of the year and ₹1,30,000 at the end. Its inventory turnover ratio is

options.text_md: 10 times
4 times
7.38 times
8 times

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** 8 times. Average inventory = (1,10,000 + 1,30,000) ÷ 2 = 1,20,000. Inventory turnover = 9,60,000 ÷ 1,20,000 = 8 times; cost, not revenue, is used because inventory is carried at cost.

questions.stem_md: Damanganga Electricals Ltd, an imagined distributor, sells partly for cash and partly on credit, and holds both book debts and bills receivable. Its trade receivables turnover ratio is computed as

options.text_md: total revenue from operations ÷ closing debtors only
net credit purchases ÷ average trade payables
cost of revenue from operations ÷ average debtors
credit revenue from operations ÷ average of (debtors + bills receivable)

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** credit revenue from operations ÷ average of (debtors + bills receivable). Only credit sales create receivables, and receivables include both debtors and bills receivable, averaged over the year.

questions.stem_md: Tawa Valley Soya Ltd, an imagined company, had revenue from operations of ₹36,00,000. At the year end its current assets were ₹7,00,000 and its current liabilities ₹2,50,000. Its working capital turnover ratio is

options.text_md: 5.14 times
14.4 times
8 times
2.8 times

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** 8 times. Working capital = 7,00,000 − 2,50,000 = 4,50,000. Working capital turnover = 36,00,000 ÷ 4,50,000 = 8 times.

questions.stem_md: The trade receivables turnover ratio of an imagined company, Sindh Valley Pottery Ltd, fell from 12 times to 8 times in a year, although it did not change the credit period it allows. The most likely reading is that

options.text_md: customers are now paying faster than before
customers are taking longer to pay, so collection has slowed down
the company has started buying more of its materials on credit
its inventory is now being sold more quickly

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** customers are taking longer to pay, so collection has slowed down. Fewer turns of receivables in a year means each rupee of credit sales stays outstanding longer, so the company should look at its collection effort.

questions.stem_md: Purna Handlooms Ltd, an imagined company, had revenue from operations of ₹18,00,000 and earned a gross profit of 25% on revenue from operations. Its inventory was ₹1,40,000 on 1 April 2025 and ₹1,60,000 on 31 March 2026. Compute its inventory turnover ratio.
questions.solution_md: Gross profit = 25% of 18,00,000 = 4,50,000; cost of revenue from operations = 18,00,000 − 4,50,000 = 13,50,000. Average inventory = (1,40,000 + 1,60,000) ÷ 2 = 1,50,000. Inventory turnover = 13,50,000 ÷ 1,50,000 = 9 times.

marking_scheme.step: Cost of revenue from operations ₹13,50,000 and average inventory ₹1,50,000

questions.stem_md: Indrayani Auto Parts Ltd, an imagined company near Pune, had total revenue from operations of ₹24,00,000, of which ₹4,00,000 was for cash. Its debtors were ₹1,50,000 on 1 April 2025 and ₹2,10,000 on 31 March 2026; its bills receivable were ₹50,000 and ₹90,000 on the same dates. Compute its trade receivables turnover ratio.
questions.solution_md: Credit revenue from operations = 24,00,000 − 4,00,000 = 20,00,000. Trade receivables: opening 2,00,000, closing 3,00,000, average 2,50,000. Turnover = 20,00,000 ÷ 2,50,000 = 8 times.

questions.stem_md: Bhadra Agro Inputs Ltd, an imagined fertiliser dealer, bought goods worth ₹15,00,000 during the year, ₹3,00,000 of them for cash. Its creditors stood at ₹1,20,000 at the start of the year and ₹1,80,000 at the end, and its bills payable at ₹40,000 and ₹60,000. How many times did it turn over its trade payables?
questions.solution_md: Net credit purchases = 15,00,000 − 3,00,000 = 12,00,000. Trade payables: opening 1,60,000, closing 2,40,000, average 2,00,000. Trade payables turnover = 12,00,000 ÷ 2,00,000 = 6 times.

questions.stem_md: For a capital-heavy business such as an imagined cement plant, the fixed asset turnover ratio is net revenue from operations divided by net ___ assets.
questions.solution_md: Net fixed assets (after depreciation) are the base: the ratio tells how much revenue each rupee invested in fixed assets brings in.

questions.stem_md: True or false? In the inventory turnover ratio of an imagined tea trader, Dikhow Tea Traders Ltd, average inventory is the opening inventory plus the closing inventory, divided by two.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** A simple average of the opening and the closing figure is used, because revenue is earned through the whole year, not only on its last day.

questions.stem_md: Match each turnover ratio in column A with the way it is computed in column B.

options.text_md: Inventory turnover ratio
Trade receivables turnover ratio
Trade payables turnover ratio
Working capital turnover ratio

match_right.text_md: Cost of revenue from operations ÷ Average inventory
Net credit purchases ÷ Average trade payables
Credit revenue from operations ÷ Average trade receivables

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(s), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Each turnover ratio sets a flow for the year against the resource that produces it: cost of sales against inventory, credit sales against receivables, credit purchases against payables, revenue against working capital.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A rising inventory turnover ratio usually shows that goods are being sold more quickly.

**Reason (R):** Inventory turnover is computed on the cost of revenue from operations rather than on revenue, because inventory is valued at cost.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both statements are true, but R only explains why cost is the numerator; it does not explain why a rising ratio means faster sales.

questions.stem_md: Ghataprabha Sugars Ltd, an imagined company in Belagavi district, had revenue from operations of ₹48,00,000 for the year. On 31 March 2026: share capital ₹12,00,000; reserves and surplus ₹6,00,000; long-term borrowings ₹6,00,000; trade payables ₹2,50,000; other current liabilities ₹50,000; property, plant and equipment (net) ₹20,00,000; inventories ₹3,80,000; trade receivables ₹2,20,000; cash and cash equivalents ₹1,00,000. Compute the fixed asset turnover, net asset (capital employed) turnover and working capital turnover ratios.
questions.solution_md: Find working capital and capital employed first (capital employed both ways must agree); each ratio then divides the same revenue by a different base.

answer.model_answer_md:
- Working capital = current assets 7,00,000 − current liabilities 3,00,000 = 4,00,000.
- Capital employed = shareholders' funds 18,00,000 + non-current liabilities 6,00,000 = 24,00,000; check: non-current assets 20,00,000 + working capital 4,00,000 = 24,00,000.

| Ratio | Formula | Working | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Fixed asset turnover | Revenue from operations ÷ Net fixed assets | 48,00,000 ÷ 20,00,000 = 2.4 times | **2.4 times** |
| Net asset turnover | Revenue from operations ÷ Capital employed | 48,00,000 ÷ 24,00,000 = 2 times | **2 times** |
| Working capital turnover | Revenue from operations ÷ Working capital | 48,00,000 ÷ 4,00,000 = 12 times | **12 times** |

questions.stem_md: Sankh Tiles Ltd, an imagined company, turned over its inventory 6 times during the year. Its revenue from operations was ₹15,00,000, on which it earned a gross profit of 20%. Its closing inventory was ₹40,000 more than its opening inventory. Find its opening and closing inventory.
questions.solution_md: Turn the gross profit rate into cost of revenue from operations, divide by the turnover to get the average, then split the average using the given difference.

answer.model_answer_md:
- Gross profit = 20% of 15,00,000 = 3,00,000; cost of revenue from operations = 15,00,000 − 3,00,000 = 12,00,000.
- Average inventory = cost ÷ inventory turnover = 12,00,000 ÷ 6 = 2,00,000.
- Opening + closing = 2 × 2,00,000 = 4,00,000, and closing − opening = 40,000.
- **Closing inventory** = (4,00,000 + 40,000) ÷ 2 = **₹2,20,000**; **opening inventory** = **₹1,80,000**.

Check: 12,00,000 ÷ 2,00,000 = 6 times.

questions.stem_md:
Sone Valley Traders Ltd, an imagined wholesaler in Dehri, gives the following for the year ended 31 March 2026. Compute its trade receivables turnover ratio and trade payables turnover ratio, and state what each one tells its management.

| Item | 1 April 2025 (₹) | 31 March 2026 (₹) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Debtors | 2,80,000 | 3,20,000 |
| Bills receivable | 1,20,000 | 80,000 |
| Creditors | 1,80,000 | 2,20,000 |
| Bills payable | 60,000 | 40,000 |

Revenue from operations: cash ₹6,00,000, credit ₹30,00,000. Purchases: cash ₹4,00,000, credit ₹24,00,000.
questions.solution_md: Use only the credit figures; trade receivables and trade payables each include the bills, averaged over the two dates.

answer.model_answer_md:
- Average trade receivables = (4,00,000 + 4,00,000) ÷ 2 = 4,00,000.
- Average trade payables = (2,40,000 + 2,60,000) ÷ 2 = 2,50,000.

| Ratio | Formula | Working | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Trade receivables turnover | Credit revenue from operations ÷ Average trade receivables | 30,00,000 ÷ 4,00,000 = 7.5 times | **7.5 times** |
| Trade payables turnover | Net credit purchases ÷ Average trade payables | 24,00,000 ÷ 2,50,000 = 9.6 times | **9.6 times** |

**Meaning:** receivables are collected about 7.5 times a year, so credit sales stay unpaid for roughly a month and a half on average; suppliers are paid about 9.6 times a year, a little faster than customers pay. The company is financing part of its customers' credit itself and should watch its collections.

questions.stem_md:
An investor is studying Yamuna Kitchenware Ltd, an imagined company in Faridabad. Its analyst has worked out these ratios for two years:

| Ratio | 2024-25 | 2025-26 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Current ratio | 2.4 : 1 | 1.3 : 1 |
| Quick ratio | 1.2 : 1 | 0.6 : 1 |
| Gross profit ratio | 28% | 30% |
| Net profit ratio (after tax) | 9% | 6% |

Interpret the change in liquidity and in profitability, and advise the investor on what to look into before deciding.
questions.solution_md: Read each pair of ratios against its benchmark and against the other year, link the two halves (higher gross margin but lower net margin), then give a reasoned recommendation.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Liquidity has weakened sharply.** The current ratio fell from 2.4 : 1 to 1.3 : 1, below the conventional 2 : 1, and the quick ratio halved from 1.2 : 1 to 0.6 : 1, below 1 : 1. Quick assets no longer cover current liabilities; the company may struggle to pay creditors on time unless it sells inventory.

**Profitability is mixed.** The gross profit ratio rose from 28% to 30%, so trading margins improved, yet the net profit ratio fell from 9% to 6%. Costs below gross profit (operating expenses, interest, perhaps on new short-term borrowing) have grown faster than revenue.

**Advice:** before investing, examine why current liabilities rose so much (short-term loans? delayed payments?), which expenses grew, and whether the fall in net margin is a one-year effect. Compare with other firms in the industry. On present evidence the investor should be cautious.

marking_scheme.step: Gross versus net profit contrast explained
